paras: The attempted lynching at Knightsville, Indiana, was a pursuit on the night of Friday, 10 July 1903, in which a posse of men tracked an unnamed Black man to his home after Mamie Goodhue accused him of trying to break into her room. The man and his family escaped before the posse could take him, leaving their belongings behind. A Brazil dispatch described the episode as a lynching "narrowly averted."

According to the Brazil correspondent of the Indianapolis Journal, Goodhue was returning from a party to her home in Knightsville when she found "a burly negro trying to break into her room." She raised the alarm, and a posse quickly gathered and traced the man to his home on the outskirts of the village. While reinforcements were being sought to take him, he and his family fled, "leaving all their belongings, behind."

A second Brazil dispatch, dated 13 July, said the man had been discovered "creeping into her room" and that the men who followed him home were "bent on lynching him." In that version the family got away through a back door.
Neither report names the man or says where the family went, and no report of an arrest of the man or of any member of the posse was found.

The Indianapolis Journal printed the incident on 12 July as a three-sentence item headed BRAZIL among its "General Indiana News," calling the pursuers a "posse" and making no mention of lynching. The Rock Island Argus in Illinois ran the wire version the next day under the subhead "Mob Spirit at Knightsville," set directly beneath a West Virginia lynching story headlined "An Awful Penalty." Both papers gave the accusation as fact and carried no statement from the man or his family.
No Black-press coverage of the incident was found.

The two accounts differ on what the man was doing, "trying to break into" the room in the Journal and "creeping into" it in the Argus. They differ also on the pursuers' aim: the Journal said only that reinforcements were sought "to take him," while the Argus wire alone stated an intent to lynch.

reader.title: Attempted lynching at Knightsville, Indiana
bases: A posse of men pursued a Black man accused of trying to enter a white woman's room to his home, by one account 'bent on lynching him', and he and his family escaped (A1, A2).

No one was killed: both reports say the man and his family got away (A1, A2). The group was a 'posse' or 'a number of men' acting on an accusation, and the Argus said a lynching was 'narrowly averted', so this was at most an attempted lynching (A2).
The Indianapolis Journal's Brazil brief and a separately worded Brazil wire in the Rock Island Argus agree on the alarm, the pursuit to the man's home and the family's escape (A1, A2).

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal Brazil correspondent
accounts.gist: A posse gathered at Goodhue's alarm and traced the man to his home; while reinforcements were sought to take him, he and his family fled, leaving their belongings.

accounts.label: Brazil wire (Rock Island Argus)
accounts.gist: Men followed the man home 'bent on lynching him'; a lynching was 'narrowly averted' when he and his family escaped through a back door.

framing.detail: The Journal ran it as a three-sentence brief among Indiana news, called the man 'a burly negro' and the pursuers a 'posse', and did not mention lynching.

The Argus printed the wire as 'Mob Spirit at Knightsville' directly below a West Virginia lynching story headlined 'An Awful Penalty', presenting the accusation as fact ('a negro was discovered ... creeping into her room').

conflicts.note: Both come from the complainant's side; no account from the man or his family appears.

versions.value: A 'posse' seeking reinforcements 'to take him'; no lynching mentioned
Men 'bent on lynching him'; a lynching 'narrowly averted'

conflicts.note: The Journal does not say what the posse meant to do with him; only the Argus wire states an intent to lynch.

record_check.dossier: Goodhue was the complainant; the target of the posse was an unnamed Black man (and his family, who fled with him).
The papers name no county; the Brazil wire says only 'this county'.
Two articles concern Knightsville (1903-07-12, 1903-07-13); the Savannah Morning News item of 1903-07-31 is about the Logansport posse.

record_check.record: Before reinforcements could take him, he and his family fled.
record_check.dossier: Supported; the family left all their belongings, and the Argus wire says the pursuers were 'bent on lynching him'.

info: Friday night, 10 July 1903 (inferred from 'Friday night' in the Sunday 12 July paper)
Knightsville, near Brazil; the man's home was in the outskirts of the village
An unnamed Black man ('a burly negro') and his family, who fled; no one was hurt
Accused of trying to break into (or 'creeping into') the room of Miss Mamie Goodhue
A 'posse' that gathered at her alarm; 'a number of men' who followed him home
The man and his family fled, through a back door, leaving all their belongings behind

set_aside: AP, Logansport, Ind., July 28: 'The posse intent on lynching the negro' who attacked Mrs. Joseph Watts; the source of the phrase the Baltimore Sun mocked (A4).
'Current Comment' quotes a Baltimore Sun editorial on an Indiana 'posse' 'intent on lynching'; the wording matches the Logansport dispatches (A3), not Knightsville.
